props.title: The Bible: In the Beginning

sections.content: John Huston's epic The Bible: In the Beginning (1966) marks an ambitious attempt to bring the first 22 chapters of Genesis to the screen. Unlike Cecil B. DeMille's The Ten Commandments (1956), which focused on Moses, Huston tackles creation, Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, Noah's Ark, and the story of Abraham. The film's scope and visual effects were groundbreaking for its time, with Huston himself playing Noah in one of cinema's most memorable portrayals of the ark builder. This kicked off a wave of biblical epics in the 1960s, including The Greatest Story Ever Told (1965) and King of Kings (1961).

sections.content: The film's practical effects deserve special mention, particularly during the Creation sequence and Noah's flood. Unlike modern CGI-heavy biblical adaptations like Noah (2014) or Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014), Huston relied on innovative practical techniques, including miniatures, matte paintings, and careful editing. The result feels more authentic than many contemporary attempts, sharing more DNA with classic epics like The Robe (1953) and Quo Vadis (1951) than modern interpretations. SUBHEAD: Biblical Storytelling Evolution

Modern biblical adaptations have taken dramatically different approaches. Darren Aronofsky's Noah (2014) reimagined the flood story as an environmental parable, while Ridley Scott's Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014) attempted to rationalize miraculous events. The Last Temptation of Christ (1988) sparked controversy with its psychological examination of Jesus, while The Passion of the Christ (2004) focused intensely on Christ's final hours. Huston's straightforward, reverent approach in The Bible: In the Beginning stands in stark contrast, treating the source material with classical Hollywood grandeur.
